html:
The Manila galleon trade was a Spanish trade route across the Pacific between Acapulco in Mexico and Manila in the Philippines, which ran from 1565 to 1815. Every year one or two large ships, the Manila galleons, carried American silver west and Asian luxury goods east.

The route depended on solving the return voyage. Ships could easily sail west from Mexico on the trade winds, but coming back was the problem until 1565, when the friar and navigator Andrés de Urdaneta found the way: sail north to catch the westerly winds and the Kuroshio current, then cross the north Pacific to California and down to Mexico. That same year Spain began settling the Philippines, which Magellan had reached in 1521 (see Magellan reaches the Philippines), and Manila was founded in 1571.

Manila was the meeting point. Chinese junks brought silk, porcelain, lacquer and other goods there, and bought silver from mines like Potosí and Zacatecas. China under the Ming had a huge demand for silver to pay taxes. The galleons then carried the Chinese goods to Acapulco, from where they went to Mexico City and on to Spain.

The voyages were long and deadly, often five or six months eastbound. But the trade joined the Americas and Asia for the first time and, with the Atlantic routes, created the first truly global trade network. It also moved people and plants: Filipinos settled in Mexico, while maize, sweet potatoes and chili peppers reached Asia. It ended in 1815, during Mexico's war of independence.
